title: Expressions, Variables & Translating Relationships
coreInsight: Algebraic symbols represent quantities and relationships; an expression describes a calculation, while an equation claims that two expressions are equal.
targetLearnerRealization: A variable names a numerical quantity; one expression can describe many cases, while an equation asserts equality and may select a particular case.
learningObjectives: Define a variable as a numerical quantity with meaningful units.
Translate fixed amounts and repeated changes into expressions.
Evaluate an expression at several variable values.
Distinguish expressions from equations and interpret equality in either direction.
Build an equation by imposing a target on a relationship.

continuity.openingCallback: Use a quick magnitude check to notice the fixed two tiles; no authored predecessor exists to quote.
closingSeeds: Find operations that preserve equality while isolating an unknown.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: A variable is merely a label for an object.
A variable always represents exactly one mystery number.
The equal sign means 'the answer comes next' rather than 'these quantities are equal'.

beats.purpose: Keep the fixed start separate from the repeated addition.
beats.expectedRealization: Keep the fixed start separate from the repeated addition.
beats.prompt: A strip starts with two tiles. Each added group contains three tiles. Without drawing the whole strip, how many tiles will it have after ten groups are added?
beats.correctFeedback: Keep the fixed start separate from the repeated addition.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Read what each number counts, then compare the operations with the story.

steps.title: Read the quantities
steps.body: Ten groups contribute ten lots of three tiles, or 30. The two starting tiles remain, so the total is 32. Counting 30 alone misses the fixed start.

resolution.takeaway: Keep the fixed start separate from the repeated addition.

visual.ariaLabel: Fixed start followed by equal added groups

beats.transitionIn: A quick size check can catch a missed piece. Here the strip grows by equal groups, but its first two tiles never disappear.

steps.title: Read the quantities
steps.body: The starting two tiles and the three tiles per group stay fixed. The number of added groups changes, so that is the quantity we name n. It can be 0, 1, 3, 10, or another whole number.

resolution.takeaway: A letter names a numerical quantity, not an object.

beats.transitionIn: The ten-group calculation works. Now keep its structure while letting the group count change.

beats.purpose: One rule can describe many different totals.

beats.prompt: Let n be the number of three-tile groups added to the two starting tiles. Which rule gives the total number of tiles?
beats.correctFeedback: One rule can describe many different totals.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Read what each number counts, then compare the operations with the story.

steps.title: Read the quantities
steps.body: There are n groups with three tiles each, giving 3 × n tiles. Add the two starting tiles to get 2 + 3n. Writing 3n means multiplication, not a two-digit number.

resolution.takeaway: One rule can describe many different totals.

beats.purpose: The variable may take several values while the relationship stays the same.
beats.expectedRealization: The variable may take several values while the relationship stays the same.

beats.correctFeedback: The variable may take several values while the relationship stays the same.

steps.title: Read the quantities
steps.body: With no groups, only the original two tiles remain. Two groups add six tiles, making eight. Five groups add fifteen tiles, making seventeen. The letter does not have one secret value throughout the story.

beats.purpose: A target turns a calculation into a claim that two quantities are equal.
beats.expectedRealization: A target turns a calculation into a claim that two quantities are equal.
beats.prompt: Now a strip must contain exactly 20 tiles. Which statement adds that condition to our rule?
beats.correctFeedback: A target turns a calculation into a claim that two quantities are equal.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Read what each number counts, then compare the operations with the story.

steps.title: Read the quantities
steps.body: The rule 2 + 3n describes a total. The statement 2 + 3n = 20 says that this total equals the required 20 tiles. It is true for n = 6: two starting tiles and six groups of three make twenty.

resolution.takeaway: A target turns a calculation into a claim that two quantities are equal.

beats.transitionIn: The rule allows many sizes. A target now asks us to select a size.

beats.purpose: Name ideas only after learners have used them.
beats.name: Variable, expression, equation
beats.conciseDefinition: A variable names a quantity. An expression describes a calculation or quantity. An equation states that two expressions have equal values.
beats.formalization: n: number of added groups; 2 + 3n: total tiles; 2 + 3n = 20: total tiles equals 20.
beats.memoryHook: Name the quantity. Describe the total. State the equality.

beats.purpose: Separate expressions from equations, including false equations and reversed equality.
beats.prompt: Sort these cards by what they are, not by whether they are true. Use n = 6 only to check their truth afterward.

response.feedback: An equals sign makes a claim of equality. A claim can be true or false; a single number is also an expression.

beats.correctFeedback: Both equality claims are equations. The other two cards are expressions.
beats.incorrectFeedback: An equation need not be true for the given value, and it need not put the calculation on the left.

steps.title: Read the quantities
steps.body: 2 + 3n and 20 name quantities. Both cards with = are equations. At n = 6, 20 = 2 + 3n is true and 2 + 3n = 19 is false. Its falsehood does not stop it being an equation.

resolution.takeaway: An equation is an equality claim, not an instruction to write an answer next.

beats.purpose: Equality compares the values on both sides.
beats.expectedRealization: Equality compares the values on both sides.
beats.prompt: A learner writes 8 + 4 = 7 + 5. What does the equals sign say?

options.text: Both sides have the same value
Only a single number may appear on the right
The right side must be calculated first

beats.correctFeedback: Equality compares the values on both sides.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Read what each number counts, then compare the operations with the story.

steps.title: Read the quantities
steps.body: Eight plus four and seven plus five both give twelve. Neither side is an instruction about the order of writing. Swapping the sides preserves the same claim.

resolution.takeaway: Equality compares the values on both sides.

beats.purpose: Start money plus weekly earnings describes savings at any whole number of weeks.
beats.expectedRealization: Start money plus weekly earnings describes savings at any whole number of weeks.
beats.prompt: Chandler receives $50, $35, and $15 for his birthday and earns $16 each week. Let w be the number of weeks worked. Which expression describes his total savings in dollars?
beats.correctFeedback: Start money plus weekly earnings describes savings at any whole number of weeks.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Read what each number counts, then compare the operations with the story.

steps.title: Read the quantities
steps.body: The gifts make a fixed start of 50 + 35 + 15 = 100 dollars. Each of w weeks adds sixteen dollars, so 16w is his paper-route earnings and 100 + 16w is his total savings. No target is needed to describe that total.

resolution.takeaway: Start money plus weekly earnings describes savings at any whole number of weeks.

visual.ariaLabel: Fixed start followed by equal added groups

beats.transitionIn: Keep the fixed start and equal groups, but let the blocks measure dollars instead of tiles.

beats.purpose: Impose the authentic target and interpret the resulting equation with arithmetic.
beats.expectedRealization: The expression becomes an equation when total savings must equal the bike price.
beats.whyNow: The approved savings story applies the start-plus-equal-groups structure after variable meaning and expression/equation distinctions have been established.
beats.entryBridge: The savings expression is ready. Now use the bike price to decide when Chandler has enough.
beats.exitBridge: The equation selected a week count; the expression still describes his savings in every week.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Fixed start plus equal weekly blocks, carried from the tile strip.
learnerPrompts: What does 16w measure, and what condition does the $500 price add?
beats.correctFeedback: Twenty-five weeks adds $400 to the $100 start, reaching $500.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Include all three gifts, then compare the money still needed with the $16 earned each week.

steps.title: Read the quantities
steps.body: Let w count weeks. The target gives 100 + 16w = 500. After the $100 start, $400 remains; $400 ÷ $16 per week = 25 weeks. Check: 100 + 16 × 25 = 500. At 24 weeks he has only $484, so 25 is the first whole week with enough. The equivalent equation 500 = 100 + 16w says exactly the same thing.

resolution.takeaway: An expression describes the savings; an equation imposes the price.

beats.purpose: Plant balance-preserving operations for A2 after consolidation.
beats.heading: Keeping an equality true
beats.body: We checked 100 + 16w = 500 using the story. For a less friendly equation, 137 + 16w = 521, guessing week counts would take more work. Next, we will find moves that simplify an equation while keeping the values on its two sides equal.

notes: Design: prior number sense supports checking the fixed start; compare concrete sizes before naming n. Tension: a letter need not be one mystery number. New realization: a relationship spans cases until an equality imposes a condition. Forward question: preserve equality while simplifying.

Beat outline: puzzle/static tile groups -> quantity choice -> rule choice -> multiple inputs -> target claim -> formal names -> statement sort -> equality comparison -> savings translation -> authentic target -> five independent transfers -> consolidation -> balance hook.
